title: 3 משחקי קופסא שעוזרים לילדים לחכות לתור

stage.need: Waiting for a turn, following one simple rule and coping with a turn that did not go your way. CDC lists 'Follows rules or takes turns when playing games with other children' at 5 years; at 4 it suggests keep teaching turn-taking.
stage.age_caveat: Milestones describe what most children do by an age, not a deadline. Some 4 year olds wait well and some 5 year olds still find it hard; the slides say בסביבות.

dev_sources.title: Milestones by 5 Years
dev_sources.publisher: CDC, Learn the Signs. Act Early.
dev_sources.quote: Follows rules or takes turns when playing games with other children / Teach your child to follow rules in games. For example, play simple board games, card games, or Simon Says. / Answers simple questions about a book or story after you read or tell it to him / Tells a story she heard or made up with at least two events. For example, a cat was stuck in a tree and a firefighter saved it / Read to your child. Ask questions, such as "What is happening in the picture?" and "What do you think will happen next?" / Encourage your child to "read" by looking at the pictures and telling the story.
dev_sources.supports: Games: following rules or taking turns in games with other children is a listed social/emotional milestone by 5 years, and CDC explicitly suggests simple board and card games as a way to teach rule-following. Books: answering questions about a book after reading and telling a story with at least two events are listed language milestones by 5; CDC's own tip is to ask 'What do you think will happen next?' while reading and to let the child 'read' by telling the story from the pictures. Caveat: CDC defines milestones as things most children (75% or more) can do by that age, so this is a typical range, not a target every child hits. Six quotes kept so you can pick; the first two are games, the rest books.

dev_sources.title: Milestones by 4 Years
dev_sources.publisher: CDC, Learn the Signs. Act Early.
dev_sources.quote: Tells what comes next in a well-known story / Read with your child. Ask him what's happening in the story and what he thinks might happen next. / Use words, such as "first," "second," and "finally." When playing, telling stories, or doing chores, ask your child what comes next. This will help your child learn about the order of events. / Continue to teach your child skills to play with others, such as using words, sharing toys, and taking turns. / Teach your child to stop and wait when excited by playing red light, green light, or freeze dance (play music, turn it off, and have everyone freeze when it stops).
dev_sources.supports: Books: 'Tells what comes next in a well-known story' is a cognitive milestone by 4 years, which maps exactly to the repetition/predict angle (the story has to be well-known, i.e. familiar). CDC recommends asking what might happen next while reading, and asking 'what comes next' when telling stories to help children learn the order of events. Games: CDC recommends teaching turn-taking as a play skill at 4, and practising stopping and waiting through games. Caveat: the stop-and-wait tip names movement games (red light green light, freeze dance), not board games; the 4-year page suggests 'simple games, such as Tic-Tac-Toe or matching games', and the rule-following milestone itself appears only on the 5-year page.

dev_sources.title: The Power of Play: A Pediatric Role in Enhancing Development in Young Children (Pediatrics 2018;142(3):e20182058)
dev_sources.publisher: American Academy of Pediatrics (Yogman, Garner, Hutchinson, Hirsh-Pasek, Golinkoff; AAP Committee on Psychosocial Aspects of Child and Family Health, Council on Communications and Media)
dev_sources.quote: Research demonstrates that developmentally appropriate play with parents and peers is a singular opportunity to promote the social-emotional, cognitive, language, and self-regulation skills that build executive function and a prosocial brain. / Peer play usually involves problem solving about the rules of the game, which requires negotiation and cooperation. / Familiar games such as “Simon Says” or “Head, Shoulders, Knees, and Toes” ask children to control their individual actions or impulses and have been shown to improve executive functioning skills.
dev_sources.supports: AAP clinical report: play with parents and peers is an opportunity to build self-regulation and executive function; peer play involves working out the rules of the game, which requires negotiation and cooperation; rule-based games that ask children to control impulses have been shown to improve executive functioning. Caveats: (1) the publisher page (publications.aap.org, DOI 10.1542/peds.2018-2058) returned 403, so the full text was read from a copy of the published PDF hosted by Sarah Lawrence College; cite it as Yogman et al., Pediatrics 2018. (2) The 'shown to improve executive functioning' evidence is about Simon Says-type impulse-control games, not board games; the report only mentions board games once ('Board games that have well-defined goals also fit into this category', i.e. guided play). (3) The report's line about learning to 'win and learn how to lose graciously' refers to rough-and-tumble play and animal data, so do NOT use it for board games. Covers young children generally, not specifically ages 4 to 5. Read from the full text of the published PDF (copy hosted at https://www.sarahlawrence.edu/cdi/pediatricsplay.pdf) because the AAP page returned 403.

dev_sources.title: How to Help Children Develop Self-Control
dev_sources.quote: Waiting helps children learn self-control. And it teaches them that others have needs, too. / Also, playing with friends offers many opportunities to help your child learn to wait, to share, and to take-turns.
dev_sources.supports: Waiting is described as practice for self-control and for understanding that others have needs; play with peers offers chances to practise waiting and turn-taking. Caveats: written for the 24 to 36 month band (older toddlers) and from 2010; it does not mention board games. Use only as general backing for 'waiting your turn is practice for self-control'.

dev_sources.title: Executive Function Activities for 5- to 7-year-olds
dev_sources.publisher: Center on the Developing Child at Harvard University
dev_sources.quote: At this age, children start to enjoy games that have rules, but do so with widely varying levels of interest and skill. / Any board game that involves some strategy provides important opportunities to make and hold a plan in mind for several moves ahead, consider the varying rules that govern different pieces, and adjust strategy in response to opponents’ moves. / As the child players become familiar with these games, try to decrease the adult role as soon as possible; the challenge is greater for children if they remember and enforce the rules independently.
dev_sources.supports: Card and board games with rules give children practice with working memory, inhibitory control and flexibility; children start to enjoy rule games around this age but vary widely; adults should step back as children learn to remember and enforce rules. Caveat: this sheet is for ages 5 to 7, so it fits the older end of a 4-5 audience; the strategy-game examples (Sorry!, checkers, mancala) are harder than typical 'simple rules' games. The 'widely varying levels of interest and skill' line is useful for honest, non-guarantee wording.

dev_sources.title: Developmental Milestones: 4 to 5 Year Olds
dev_sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org (American Academy of Pediatrics), from Caring for Your Baby and Young Child: Birth to Age 5, 7th ed.
dev_sources.quote: More likely to agree to rules / Recalls part of a story / Tells longer stories
dev_sources.supports: AAP's 4 to 5 milestone list: under Social milestones, 'More likely to agree to rules'; under Language milestones, 'Recalls part of a story' and 'Tells longer stories'. Fits the exact 4 to 5 age band. Caveat: these are short list items about typical development, not claims that games or books cause these skills.

popularity_signals.description: Position 5 of 441 in the board-games collection. Toys R Us Israel board-games collection (441 products) sorted by the site's own 'הנמכרים ביותר' option; a sales sort with an undisclosed time window, not a published chart. Position re-read on 2026-10-08 from the sorted pages.
Sold by 3 independent Israeli retailers besides the publisher: Toys R Us Israel, ToyHouse, Center Toys.
Published in Hebrew by Kodkod, a long-established Israeli game publisher; featured on Kodkod's home page product grid on the access date.

products.popularity_reasoning: One strong Israel-specific ranking signal (5th of 441 board games at Toys R Us Israel by the store's own best-selling sort), plus multi-retailer availability and an established Israeli publisher. Meets the rule on the ranking alone.
products.developmental_relevance: Every turn is spin, count, pull, so the rule is concrete and visible. The suspense (any carrot might launch the rabbit) keeps the waiting child watching other players' turns instead of drifting, and the spinner decides how many carrots you take, so the child has to accept a number they did not choose.
products.parent_tip_source: Your suggestion: let the child hold the spinner and hand it to the next player out loud ('עכשיו התור של אבא'), and count each carrot together. For a 4-year-old who struggles with losing, play that everyone who is still holding carrots when the rabbit jumps gets a cheer, and the catcher spins first next round.

products.popularity_reasoning: A solid Israel-specific ranking signal (28th of 441 board games, 37th of ~2,968 kids' games at Toys R Us Israel by the store's best-selling sort) plus independent multi-retailer availability and an established Israeli publisher: two or more independent signals.
products.developmental_relevance: Only one hand touches the tree at a time, so the child has to keep hands off while others pull, and the die decides which colour stick is allowed. Kodkod's own text spells out the care rule ('ז-ה-י-ר-ו-ת שהקופים לא יפלו!'), which turns waiting into watching and planning which stick to try next.
products.parent_tip_source: Your suggestion: pass a 'turn token' (a toy or spoon) to whoever is pulling, and only the token holder may touch the tree. With a younger 4-year-old, skip the die at first and let them pick any stick, then add the colour rule once they wait well.

image.rights_note: ToyHouse og:image: flat front photo of the shrink-wrapped Hebrew Kodkod box (slight glare). Kodkod's own image is only 270x270. No press or licence terms seen on either page.

products.limitations: Sold out at Toys R Us Israel on the access date (in stock at ToyHouse and listed at Kodkod and Center Toys). Toys R Us text says 'מתאים לגילאי 3 שנים ומעלה' while box says 4-99; both fit 4-5. Zap shows one product review ('חוות דעת (1)') that I could not open. Mechanically it shares a 'pull and see what happens' moment with משוך בגזר, but here the outcome depends on the child's steady hand, while in משוך בגזר it is pure luck.

claims.wording_he: משחקי קופסא שעוזרים לילדים לחכות לתור
claims.supports: CDC 5 years: teach your child to follow rules in games, for example simple board games; ZERO TO THREE: playing with others gives many chances to learn to wait and take turns.

claims.wording_he: בסביבות גיל 5 הרבה ילדים כבר מחכים לתור
claims.supports: CDC 5-year milestone: follows rules or takes turns when playing games with other children; AAP lists 'more likely to agree to rules' at 4 to 5.
Harvard: children start to enjoy games with rules 'with widely varying levels of interest and skill'; CDC tip: teach rules with simple board games. 'Short turn, one rule' is our reading of 'simple'.
